Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let  
\[
k=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor .
\]

First, check that \(n=1230\) works. Since
\[
35^2=1225\le 1230<1296=36^2,
\]
we have \(k=35\), and
\[
1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41.
\]

- Modulo \(2,3,5\): \(35!\) is divisible by each of \(2,3,5\), so \((35!)^{1230!}\) is divisible by them, and \(450\) is also divisible by them.
- Modulo \(41\): \(41\nmid 35!\), and \(40\mid 1230!\). By Fermat’s little theorem,
\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1 \pmod{41}.
\]
Also \(450\equiv -1\pmod{41}\), so
\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 0\pmod{41}.
\]
Thus \(1230\) divides the expression.

Now suppose \(n>1230\) is a solution, and let \(k=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\). Then \(k\ge 35\).

Take any prime \(p\mid n\).

- If \(p\le k\), then \(p\mid k!\), so \((k!)^{n!}\equiv 0\pmod p\). Hence \(p\mid 450\), so \(p\in\{2,3,5\}\). Moreover, the exponents must satisfy
\[
v_2(n)\le 1,\qquad v_3(n)\le 2,\qquad v_5(n)\le 2,
\]
because otherwise \((k!)^{n!}\) would be divisible by a higher power than \(450\).

- If \(p>k\), then \(p\nmid k!\). Since \(p\mid n\), we have \(p-1\mid n!\). By Fermat’s little theorem,
\[
(k!)^{n!}\equiv 1\pmod p,
\]
so \(p\mid 451=11\cdot 41\).

If \(k\ge 41\), the second case cannot occur, so \(n\le 2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2=450\), impossible. Thus \(35\le k\le 40\).

In this range, \(11\le k\), so \(11\nmid n\). If \(41\nmid n\), again \(n\le 450\), impossible. Hence \(41\mid n\). Since \(n<41^2\), write \(n=41t\). Also
\[
1225\le n\le 1680 \implies 30\le t\le 40.
\]
The allowed form of \(t\) is
\[
t=2^a3^b5^c,\qquad a\le 1,\ b\le 2,\ c\le 2.
\]
The only such \(t\) in \([30,40]\) is \(t=30\), giving \(n=41\cdot 30=1230\), contradicting \(n>1230\).

Therefore the largest possible \(n\) is

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
